items.title: An open-source AI Scrum Team that lives natively in GitHub Issues
items.raw_excerpt:
Hi HN,
I've been experimenting a lot with autonomous coding agents (like OpenClaw and various CLI tools), but I kept running into two major roadblocks when trying to use them for actual production work:
Security & State: Most agents require running a persistent state on a local machine or VPS, often needing broad file system access. It's a security nightmare for enterprise code.
Chaos: Generalist agents try to do everything at once (planning, coding, testing) in a single context window, which inevitably leads to hallucinations and broken dependencies.
I wanted a system that mirrored how actual engineering teams work, so I built an open-source framework that runs entirely inside GitHub.

Prologue | One Person, One Company: The Fourth Wave of Individual Economy Is Erupting

Every reconstruction of production relations in history has emerged from the collision between the bottlenecks of old organizational forms and the power of new technologies. From the street vendors of the 1980s, to the legal entities established by the 1999 "Sole Proprietorship Enterprise Law," and then to the mobile internet wave of "mass entrepreneurship and innovation" in 2014—each leap in China's individual economy policy has been a collective response to the times.

Today, with the widespread adoption of infrastructure like Agent and OpenClaw, super entrepreneurs are presented with a natural opportunity to drive innovation and transformation based on AI technology. Innovative models such as OPC (One Person Company) and SE (Super Entrepreneur) are propelling the arrival of the fourth wave.

The data already tells this story: according to the "2025 China Digital Economy Entrepreneurship White Paper," over 12 million entrepreneurs nationwide have chosen the OPC model, with new OPC registrations increasing by 47% year-on-year, creating 23% of the total economic value in the new economy. The super individual is becoming the smallest yet most efficient unit of the innovative economy.

SE super entrepreneurs are not "individual businesses" in the traditional sense, nor are they digital replicas of freelancers. They represent a new organizational paradigm of "individual + AI = company"—an individual with keen insight and core professional capabilities, leveraging large models, intelligent agents, and low-code platforms.

excerpt_i18n.en: Before the "lobster" could be fattened, "paying to have the lobster uninstalled" has recently become a new business in the AI circle. This actually reflects a practical issue: when we integrate AI Agents into real workflows, they are not as "capable" as imagined. They can initiate tasks but often face repeated interruptions during execution; they lose context and become inconsistent in multi-turn conversations; they struggle to accurately call external tools for non-standard demands; and after someone grants permissions, they might wake up to find emails cleared and thousands of dollars in tokens burned. In previous discussions with multiple AI hardware and application-layer entrepreneurs, a painful consensus emerged: current AI Agents are more like "showcasing single-point skills" rather than "getting work done." They excel at writing copy, drawing images, or running code snippets, but when it comes to end-to-end management of real business processes or long-chain academic tasks, their shortcomings are exposed. Ultimately, the problem lies not in the form of the Agent but in the underlying large models themselves, which still lack stable and reliable "execution capabilities." For Agents to truly enter workflows, this hurdle must be overcome. Large models must cross a watershed: evolving from passive "single-generation feedback" to active "task decomposition and organized execution." With this question in mind, we decided to test in a way closer to real usage scenarios—by assembling a "Journey to the West pilgrimage team" to see how far the MiniMax M2.7 model can advance tasks through division of labor and collaboration. 01&nb

items.raw_excerpt: 现如今，扩散模型已经成为当前图像生成领域的核心技术之一。从文本生成图像到复杂视觉内容合成，这类模型已经能够生成高度逼真的画面。然而，在真实应用场景中，人们对生成模型的要求并不仅仅是“生成逼真图像”，而是希望模型能够严格按照提示完成特定任务。 例如，在要求生成包含指定文字的图像时，模型可能 simply 将文字放大到占据画面大部分区域，从而轻松获得 OCR 系统的高分，而在需要生成多个对象的任务中，模型也可能通过极度简化场景结构来满足评分规则。这种现象通常被称为“奖励作弊”，已经成为当前生成模型对齐研究中的一个重要挑战。 为了解决这一问题，近年来一些研究开始尝试利用强化学习或奖励机制对扩散模型进行后训练，希望通过奖励信号引导模型生成更加符合任务要求的内容。然而实践中逐渐发现，这种方法容易带来一个新的问题：模型可能学会迎合评价指标，而不是理解任务本身。 在这样的研究背景下，香港大学赵恒爽团队提出了一种新的扩散模型后训练方法，并在论文《GDRO: Group-level Reward Post-training Suitable for Diffusion Models》中系统探讨了这一问题。研究通过引入组级奖励优化机制对扩散模型进行后训练，在提升模型任务表现的同时有效缓解奖励作弊问题，并且还可以显著提高训练效率。 更重要的，这一方法在实际应用中也具有明显的工程价值。传统的在线强化学习方法通常需要在每一次优化步骤中重新执行完整的扩散采样过程来生成图像，这意味着模型需要不断运行完整的扩散链进行图像生成，在线采样往往成为训练过程中最主要的时间和计算开销。 相比之下，GDRO 支持完全离线的训练方式，在训练开始之前先生成并保存带有评分信息的图像数据，之后的优化过程无需再依赖扩散采样，从而避免了重复执行扩散链带来的巨大计算成本。同时，这个方法也不依赖特定的扩散采样器，不需要通过 ODE

excerpt_i18n.en:
Today, diffusion models have become one of the core technologies in the field of image generation. From text-to-image synthesis to the creation of complex visual content, these models are capable of producing highly realistic images. However, in real-world applications, the demand for generative models goes beyond merely "generating realistic images"; there is an expectation for models to strictly follow prompts to accomplish specific tasks. For instance, when tasked with generating images containing specified text, a model might simply enlarge the text to occupy most of the image area, thereby easily achieving high scores from OCR systems. Similarly, in tasks requiring the generation of multiple objects, a model might overly simplify the scene structure to meet scoring criteria. This phenomenon, often referred to as "reward hacking," has become a significant challenge in current generative model alignment research.

To address this issue, recent studies have begun exploring the use of reinforcement learning or reward mechanisms for post-training diffusion models, aiming to guide them toward generating content that better aligns with task requirements through reward signals. However, it has gradually become apparent in practice that this approach can lead to a new problem: models may learn to cater to evaluation metrics rather than truly understanding the task itself.

Against this research backdrop, the team led by Hengshuang Zhao at the University of Hong Kong has proposed a new post-training method for diffusion models. In their paper "GDRO: Group-level Reward Post-training Suitable for Diffusion Models," they systematically investigate this issue.
excerpt_i18n.es: Hoy en día, los modelos de difusión se han convertido en una de las tecnologías centrales en el campo de la generación de imágenes. Desde la generación de imágenes a partir de texto hasta la síntesis de contenido visual complejo, estos modelos son capaces de producir escenas altamente realistas. Sin embargo, en aplicaciones prácticas, las expectativas hacia los modelos generativos no se limitan a "crear imágenes realistas", sino que se espera que cumplan tareas específicas siguiendo estrictamente las indicaciones. Por ejemplo, al solicitar una imagen que contenga texto específico, el modelo podría simplemente ampliar el texto hasta ocupar la mayor parte de la escena, logrando así fácilmente una alta puntuación en sistemas OCR, mientras que en tareas que requieren múltiples objetos, el modelo también podría simplificar excesivamente la estructura de la escena para cumplir con los criterios de evaluación.

excerpt_i18n.en: Many machine learning systems are designed under the premise that once a model is trained, its parameters are essentially fixed. Regardless of the input data, the model relies on the same set of parameters for inference. This paradigm has been highly successful over the past decade, with improvements in model capabilities primarily driven by larger model sizes, more data, and longer training times. However, as artificial intelligence gradually enters more complex application environments, this "fixed-parameter" approach is beginning to show limitations. Real-world tasks often exhibit high diversity, with different user needs and task objectives that may even conflict with each other. For example, in image editing scenarios, the same image may correspond to entirely different modification requirements. Some tasks require enhancing details, such as deblurring or image restoration, while others require reducing details, such as adding blur effects or simulating the aging process of old photos. If a model always relies on the same set of parameters, it often has to compromise between different objectives, thereby affecting the final outcome. In the past, researchers typically addressed this issue through domain adaptation or model fine-tuning. When a model enters a new domain, it needs to be retrained or its parameters adjusted to adapt to the new data distribution. However, this approach often entails additional training costs and increases the complexity of system deployment and maintenance. Is there an opportunity to achieve real-time adaptation? excerpt_i18n.es: Muchos sistemas de aprendizaje automático parten de una premisa en su diseño: una vez entrenado el modelo, sus parámetros son básicamente fijos. Independientemente de los datos de entrada, el modelo depende del mismo conjunto de parámetros para realizar la inferencia. Este paradigma ha tenido mucho éxito en la última década, y la mejora de la capacidad del modelo se ha basado principalmente en un mayor tamaño del modelo, más datos y un entrenamiento más prolongado. Sin embargo, a medida que la inteligencia artificial se adentra en entornos de aplicación más complejos, este enfoque de "parámetros fijos" comienza a mostrar limitaciones.
